t: Lok Adalats derive their statutory status from:
e: The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 gave statutory status to Lok Adalats pursuant to Article 39-A of the Constitution; their proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings.

t: The Motor Vehicles Act was first enacted in India in the year:
e: The first Motor Vehicles Act was enacted in 1939; it was replaced by the MV Act 1988, which has since been amended (1994, 2000, 2001, 2019, etc.).

t: Section 163A of the MV Act, which was deleted by the 2019 amendment, dealt with:
o: Interim relief under the Solatium Scheme
Compensation on a structured formula basis with the Second Schedule
e: Section 163A (structured formula compensation with Schedule II, last amended by notification of 22.05.2018) was omitted; fixed no-fault compensation is now under s.164.

t: Under Section 164, the fixed compensation payable in the case of death is:
e: Section 164 provides ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt, payable by the owner or insurer without proof of wrongful act or neglect.

t: Under the pre-amendment Section 161, hit-and-run compensation for death and grievous hurt was respectively:
e: The old Solatium Scheme amounts were ₹25,000 (death) and ₹12,500 (grievous hurt); the 2019 amendment raised these to ₹2 lakh and ₹50,000 and dropped the term 'Solatium Fund'.

t: The Motor Vehicle Accident Fund constituted under Section 164B comprises:
o: An Account for Insured Vehicles, an Account for Uninsured Vehicles and a Hit and Run Compensation Fund
A Death Account and an Injury Account
A Solatium Fund and a Golden Hour Fund
A Central Account and separate State Accounts
e: The Fund has three accounts: Account for Insured Vehicles, Account for Uninsured Vehicles and the Hit and Run Compensation Fund, held by a Trust and administered by GIC.

t: Under Section 164 of the amended MV Act, the fixed no-fault compensation payable for grievous hurt is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 164 fixes ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt, payable without proof of negligence. Nothing is payable under s.164 for minor injury.

t: After the 2019 amendment, no appeal lies against an award of the Claims Tribunal if the amount in dispute in the appeal is less than:
e: Section 173(2) was amended to raise the threshold from ten thousand rupees to one lakh rupees.

t: Under the amended Section 159, the police officer must prepare and submit the accident information report to the Claims Tribunal within:
e: Section 159 requires the police officer, during investigation, to prepare an accident information report in the prescribed form within three months and submit it to the Claims Tribunal and other prescribed agency.

t: The time allowed to the insurer for filing its written statement before the Claims Tribunal in a claim petition is:
e: The trainers' limitation table lists 90 days for filing the written statement, 6 months for filing the claim petition and 90 days for appeal against the award.

t: The offence of rash or negligent driving on a public way, formerly Section 279 IPC, is now covered by:
e: Section 279 IPC maps to Section 281 BNS 2023. Section 106 is causing death by negligence, Section 125 is endangering life or personal safety, and Section 303 is theft.

t: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from:
e: BNS 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024, along with the BNSS and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam.

t: The Pranay Sethi case was decided by a Constitution Bench of five judges on:
e: Pranay Sethi (31.10.2017) standardised future prospects for self-employed and fixed-salary persons, personal-expense deductions and the conventional heads.

t: The multiplier applicable where the deceased was aged between 56 and 60 years is:
e: After age 50 the multiplier reduces by two per band: 11 (51–55), 9 (56–60), 7 (61–65) and 5 (66–70).

t: For a self-employed deceased aged between 40 and 50 years, the addition for future prospects under Pranay Sethi is:
e: Self-employed/fixed-salary: 40% below 40, 25% for 40–50, 10% above 50. The corresponding salaried-permanent figures are 50%, 30% and 15%.

t: Under Section 2 of the MV Act, a 'light motor vehicle' is a transport vehicle or omnibus whose gross vehicle weight, or a motor car/tractor/road-roller whose unladen weight, does not exceed:
e: LMV: GVW/ULW up to 7,500 kg; medium vehicle 7,501–12,000 kg; heavy vehicle above 12,000 kg.

t: After the 2019 amendment, a driving licence to drive a transport vehicle is valid for:
e: Section 14 as amended: transport vehicle licence 5 years (earlier 3); for dangerous/hazardous goods 3 years (earlier 1). Non-transport licences are now age-banded.

t: Which Chapter of the MV Act, dealing with 'Liability without fault in certain cases' (Sections 140–144), was deleted by the 2019 amendment?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Chapter X (Sections 140–144) on no-fault interim liability was omitted; no-fault compensation is now a fixed, final payment under the new Section 164 in Chapter XI.

t: Under the detailed accident report scheme, the Detailed Accident Report (Form VII) must be submitted by the Investigating Officer to the Claims Tribunal within:
e: FAR within 48 hours, Form II to victims within 10 days, driver/owner Forms III and IV within 30 days, IAR (Form V) within 50 days, victim Forms VI-A/VI-B within 60 days and DAR (Form VII) within 90 days.

t: With effect from the IRDAI circular of 18 October 2023, legal liability to employees of the insured travelling in or driving a private car (IMT-29) is:
o: Available only under the Own Damage section
An inbuilt compulsory cover under the third party liability section of a private car policy without additional premium
An optional endorsement at ₹50 additional premium per employee
Excluded from all private car policies
e: IMT-29 was earlier an optional add-on at ₹50 extra premium; from October 2023 it is inbuilt in the TP liability section of private car package, bundled and stand-alone liability policies.

t: A pedestrian crossing a highway at an unmarked spot at night is hit by an overspeeding car. The Tribunal finds the pedestrian 25% responsible. Assessed compensation is ₹20,00,000. The award against the insurer would be:
o: ₹20,00,000, since contributory negligence is not a defence under the MV Act
Nil, as the pedestrian was at fault
e: Where the victim's own lack of care contributes to the accident, compensation is reduced in proportion to the contributory negligence found: 20,00,000 less 25% = ₹15,00,000.

topic: Third party – who is a third party
t: A cleaner of a goods truck is injured while the truck is in motion due to the driver's negligence. After the 2019 amendment, under the Act policy he is:
o: A third party, since 'third party' now includes the driver and any co-worker on a transport vehicle
Not covered because he was not carrying goods
Covered only if a Workmen's Compensation endorsement was taken
A gratuitous passenger excluded from cover
e: Section 145(i) as amended includes the driver and any other co-worker on a transport vehicle as third parties; the earlier requirement to pay extra premium for named employees under the WC Act was deleted.

t: An insurer settles 60 pending MACT claims at a National Lok Adalat. Which advantage of this forum is NOT correct?
o: Settlement is speedy and economical to the parties
It reduces the backlog of cases before the Tribunal
The award is based on consent and is final
Awards can be challenged in appeal before the High Court within 90 days
e: Lok Adalat awards are consent-based and final; no appeal lies. Speed, economy, finality and unburdening of courts are the recognised advantages.

t: On receiving information of an accident, what is the first statutory step the insurer must take under Section 149(1)?
o: Lodge a complaint with the police under Section 134
Deposit ₹5,00,000 with the Tribunal under Section 164
Designate an officer to settle the claims relating to that accident
File a written statement before the Tribunal within 90 days
e: Section 149(1) requires the insurer, upon receiving information of the accident from the claimant, the accident information report or otherwise, to designate an officer to settle the claims.

t: Under Pranay Sethi, for a deceased below 40 years holding a permanent job, the addition for future prospects is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Salaried persons on a permanent job get 50% (below 40), 30% (40–50) and 15% (above 50). Self-employed or fixed-salary persons get 40%, 25% and 10% respectively.

t: A car owner pays the TP premium by cheque which is dishonoured; the vehicle is involved in a fatal accident the next day. The insurer's position under Section 150(2):
o: The insurer is liable because a certificate of insurance was issued
Non-receipt of premium under Section 64VB of the Insurance Act is a specified defence
The insurer must pay and recover from the owner under Section 149(4)
The insurer is liable for ₹5 lakh only under Section 164
e: The 2019 amendment added non-receipt of premium (s.64VB) and drunken driving (s.185) to the defences under s.150(2); the statutory pay-and-recover provision of old s.149(4) was deleted.

t: Which of the following is NOT a defence available to the insurer under Section 150(2) of the amended MV Act?
o: The driver was overspeeding at the time of the accident
The policy was obtained by non-disclosure of a material fact
The driver was under the influence of alcohol as laid down in Section 185
The vehicle was used for organised racing or speed testing
e: Mere negligence such as overspeeding is the very risk insured and is not a defence; s.150(2) lists specified breaches (use, driver, war risks), voidness for non-disclosure, non-receipt of premium and drunken driving.

t: Under the amended Section 150, which party has a statutory duty to inform the Tribunal whether the vehicle was insured on the date of the accident and with which insurer?
e: The amended section casts a duty on the owner to furnish to the Tribunal or court the information as to whether the vehicle was insured on the date of accident and the name of the insurer.

t: A person suffers a fractured femur (grievous hurt) in an accident caused by an unidentified vehicle in 2024. The compensation payable under the hit-and-run provisions is:
e: Hit-and-run grievous hurt compensation is ₹50,000 under the amended s.161 (₹2 lakh for death), paid through the Hit and Run Compensation Fund.

t: A claimant files under Section 164 for a fracture-free laceration on the arm (simple hurt) and claims ₹2,50,000. The correct position is:
o: No compensation is payable under Section 164 for simple injuries
₹25,000 is payable as under the old Section 163A
Compensation is payable only after proof of negligence
e: Section 164 covers only death (₹5 lakh) and grievous hurt (₹2.5 lakh); unlike old s.163A, there is no fixed amount for minor injury.

t: A legal heir approaches an advocate 11 months after a fatal accident that occurred in 2024 to file a claim petition under Section 166. The position is:
o: The petition is within time, since no limitation applies to MACT claims
The petition is within time, as the limitation is two years
The petition is beyond the six-month limitation; the Tribunal would have to be moved for condonation of delay
The claim is permanently barred with no remedy
e: The amended s.166(3) requires filing within six months of the accident; a belated petition needs condonation of delay by the Tribunal.

t: An injured claimant with a pending Section 166 petition dies of a heart attack unconnected with the accident injuries. Under the amended Act:
o: The claim abates completely under Section 306 of the Indian Succession Act
The right to claim compensation for the injury survives to his legal representatives irrespective of whether the death had any nexus with the injury
Only the medical expenses already incurred can be claimed by the heirs
The claim survives only if death was caused by the accident injuries
e: The 2019 amendment to s.166 provides that the right to claim compensation for injury survives to the legal representatives whether or not the cause of death is related to the injury.

t: A goods carriage of GVW 2,800 kg is involved in an accident and the insurer wishes to plead that the vehicle had no permit. The plea would fail because:
o: The insurer cannot raise permit-related defences under any circumstances
Permits are needed only for passenger vehicles
A goods vehicle with GVW up to 3,000 kg does not require a permit
Permits are issued only to vehicles above 7,500 kg
e: Section 66(3) exempts certain transport vehicles from the permit requirement, including goods carriages with GVW not exceeding 3,000 kg, so absence of permit is not a breach.

t: Deduction for health insurance premium under Section 80D for an individual below 60 years (self and family) is up to:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹25,000; ₹50,000 where the insured is a senior citizen; an additional ₹25,000/₹50,000 for parents.

t: A stage carriage permit was issued on 01.04.2021. Unless renewed, it remains effective up to:
e: Under Section 81 a permit is effective for five years from the date of issue or renewal; temporary permits under s.87 are for a maximum of four months.

t: After an accident causing injury, the driver of the insured vehicle must, under Section 134:
o: Only lodge an FIR within 48 hours
Only pay the medical expenses of the injured
Secure medical attention for the injured, give information to the police and give written information of the accident and policy details to the insurer
Only report the matter to the RTO within 30 days
e: Section 134 casts duties on the driver: take reasonable steps for medical attention, give information required by the police, and give the insurer written information regarding the accident and the policy.

t: The owner of a goods carriage commits a technical breach (driver's licence expired by two months). A pedestrian is killed. Following the Supreme Court's reiteration in 2025 (K. Nagendra), the insurer:
o: Need pay only ₹5 lakh under Section 164
Pays only if the owner is untraceable
Must first pay the full compensation to the victim's family and then recover from the owner
e: The Supreme Court has repeatedly reaffirmed 'pay and recover': even where the owner is in breach, the insurer first satisfies the award to the third party victim and recovers from the owner.

t: A deceased leaves behind his wife, two minor children and his aged father. Following Magma General Insurance v. Nanu Ram (2018), consortium is payable to:
o: The father only, as the eldest claimant
The wife and the children only
The wife only, as spousal consortium
All four claimants – spousal, parental (to each child) and filial (to the father)
e: Magma v. Nanu Ram extended Pranay Sethi's consortium to parental consortium for children and filial consortium for parents, each at the Pranay Sethi amount.

t: The Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025 is implemented through designated hospitals with which nodal agency and IT platform?
o: State Road Safety Council as nodal agency, using the National Health Authority's IT platform
IRDAI as nodal agency, using the IIB portal
GIC Re as nodal agency, using the Parivahan portal
The Claims Tribunal as nodal agency, using e-Courts
e: The 2025 Scheme (notified 5 May 2025) is managed by the State Road Safety Council in coordination with the National Health Authority, whose IT platform handles registration, verification and claims.

t: A salaried permanent employee aged 48, earning ₹50,000 per month, dies leaving wife, three children and both parents. Loss of dependency as per Pranay Sethi is:
e: 6,00,000 + 30% future prospects (salaried, 40–50) = 7,80,000; six dependants → deduct 1/4 = 5,85,000; × multiplier 13 (46–50) = ₹76,05,000.

t: A self-employed deceased aged 58 earning ₹40,000 per month leaves a wife and two children. Loss of dependency is:
A 38-year-old private school teacher on a fixed salary (not a permanent job) earning ₹18,000 per month dies, leaving wife, four children and both parents. Loss of dependency is:
e: 2,16,000 + 40% (fixed salary, below 40) = 3,02,400; seven dependants → deduct 1/5 = 2,41,920; × multiplier 15 (36–40) = ₹36,28,800.

t: In a 2019 death claim the deceased leaves only his wife. Under Pranay Sethi the amount under conventional heads (before any enhancement) is:
e: Loss of estate 15,000 + spousal consortium 40,000 + funeral 15,000 = ₹70,000 at the base 2017 rates.

t: A Tribunal awards ₹20,00,000 with 7.5% simple interest from the petition date; interest accrues for exactly two years. Two claimants share equally and both have furnished PAN. TDS deducted from each claimant's interest is:
e: Interest = 20,00,000 × 7.5% × 2 = 3,00,000; each claimant's share 1,50,000 exceeds ₹50,000, so TDS at 10% (PAN available) = ₹15,000 each.

t: An award of ₹12,00,000 carries 7.5% simple interest for 365 days, shared equally by four claimants. The TDS position on interest is:
o: No TDS, as each claimant's interest of ₹22,500 does not exceed ₹50,000
e: Interest = 90,000; per claimant 22,500, below the ₹50,000 threshold, so no TDS is deducted.

t: Third-party insurance is compulsory for a motor vehicle used in a public place under which section of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 146 makes TP cover compulsory; Section 164 fixes no-fault compensation (₹5 lakh death / ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt).

t: A Tribunal awards ₹40,000 to a claimant for a minor injury. The insurer wants to appeal. The position is:
o: No appeal lies, since the amount in dispute is less than ₹1,00,000
e: Under s.173(2) as amended, no appeal lies where the amount in dispute is less than one lakh rupees; the deposit rule (₹25,000 or 50%, whichever is less) applies only where an appeal is maintainable.

t: A self-employed deceased aged 45 earning ₹20,000 per month has his mother as the only dependant. Annual loss of dependency (multiplicand) and multiplier are:
e: 20,000 + 25% = 25,000 per month; bachelor-type deduction of 1/2 for a single parent → 12,500 × 12 = 1,50,000; multiplier for age 41–45 is 14 (loss of dependency ₹21,00,000).

t: Accident on 08.11.2023; the deceased leaves wife, one major son and one unmarried daughter. Applying Pranay Sethi with Magma v. Nanu Ram and 10% enhancement per three-year span, the conventional heads total:
e: Six years since October 2017 = two spans = +20%. Consortium 48,000 × 3 = 1,44,000; loss of estate 18,000; funeral 18,000; total ₹1,80,000.

t: In one accident caused by an insured truck, one person dies, one suffers grievous hurt and two suffer simple injuries. Total no-fault compensation payable under Section 164 is:
e: Death ₹5,00,000 + grievous hurt ₹2,50,000 = ₹7,50,000; simple injuries attract nothing under s.164.
